reasoning: Both outputs satisfy all four expectations and neither fabricates evidence, so the decision turns on density and on how fast the user reaches something pasteable. A leads with an unmissable 'The rule block — paste this' heading at ~24% of its length, containing one self-contained fenced block (DB-001/DB-002, each with Rule / Precedent / Self-check) that can go straight into a project rules file. B's deliverable is diffuse: a _TEMPLATE.sql, four lines of rules prose, a hook script, a settings.json fragment and a checker self-test, spread across three tiers and gated behind a 20-minute 'reproduce it before you fix it' step — so a 30-second skim yields a project rather than a paste. On expectation 3, A's diagnosis is the deeper one (storage / durability / enforcement, plus 'your correction arrives after the migration is written — it's a repair, not an instruction'), and its 'an assertion is argued with, evidence is only disproven' plus the argument for using the token `down` rather than the phrase 'rollback step' are non-obvious mechanisms for why a rule survives. On expectation 4, A is directly on-criterion: it ranks four homes explicitly by whether each is loaded at the moment a migration is written, names the context budget, and identifies the weak-pointer failure ('See docs/precedents/database.md' gets read roughly never because nothing says when). B's placement section is framed as tier selection rather than loadedness, though its skill-description trap is a good catch. B is not weak — 'there were never six corrections, there were six sessions that each got told once' is the single sharpest line in either document, its PostToolUse exit-2 hook semantics are correct, its [[:space:]] classes are more portable than A's \s, and giving the checker its own self-test (disclosing that the first regex rejected files produced by its own template) is a genuine deepening that A lacks. But roughly 200 of B's extra 222 lines are not all load-bearing: 'Common mistakes with this specific fix' restates five points already argued, 'Order of operations' restates the tiers a third time, and assumption four is flagged four separate times (opening table, Step 1, leak table, Stress Test). B also carries a mild internal tension — 'Six is a pattern. Build the permanent thing' immediately followed by a step telling you not to build yet. On honesty about evidence both behave well, but A's is structural rather than only commentary: it deliberately leaves the Precedent dates and verbatim quote as blanks and argues why filling them from imagination would be worse ('a precedent invented at the desk is a stale line wearing armour'), then supplies a recovery grep. I checked A's one concrete verification claim — it states 92 transcript files mention the term; running the same command now returns 98, consistent with a real run whose count has since grown. A ran what it claimed to run. A's deductions are minor: its CI grep '^\s*(pass|-- *TODO)\s*$' can false-positive on a bare `pass` line inside an up-block, and its zsh-globbing aside is directionally right but imprecise (zsh errors on no-match rather than silently finding nothing).

strengths: Pasteable rule block arrives early under an unmissable 'paste this' heading; one self-contained artifact rather than five
Self-check lives inside the rule text itself (up -> down -> up round trip, plus a count-match test: files changed must equal files round-tripped clean)
Strongest account of why bare imperatives decay: assertions lose to plausible local arguments, and evidence beside the rule is what resists softening
Distinctive durability mechanics: stable citable IDs that are never renumbered, and using the token `down` rather than the phrase 'rollback step' so rule vocabulary matches file vocabulary
Placement section ranked explicitly by whether the rule is loaded at the moment of writing, including the weak-pointer failure mode and the context-budget tradeoff
Anticipates the exception that kills the rule (DB-002 for irreversible migrations) instead of leaving an exemption clause

Deliberately leaves the precedent slots blank with a clear argument against inventing one, plus a working recovery grep; its stated verification (92 matching transcripts) checks out against a live run returning 98
Stress test names the real weakness (precedent bought by irritation, not by an incident) and the strongest alternative hypothesis (the codebase's existing migrations teach the opposite of the rule)
weaknesses: CI script's '^\s*(pass|-- *TODO)\s*$' can match a bare `pass` line anywhere in the file, not just an empty down-block
\s in ERE is a GNU extension and would fail on stock BSD grep (moot on this machine, which shims grep to ugrep)
zsh globbing aside is slightly wrong: unquoted *.jsonl errors with 'no matches found' rather than silently matching nothing
No equivalent of B's checker self-test, so its CI gate could rot into a meaningless green check
No measurement protocol to confirm the rule actually stuck beyond 'say DB-001 and see'

Richest verification apparatus: template VERIFIED checkboxes, a PostToolUse hook with correct exit-2 blocking semantics, CI reuse, and a self-test for the checker itself
Honest disclosure that the first regex draft matched '-- ROLLBACK' but not '-- ## ROLLBACK', rejecting files its own template produced
Makes the irreversible case a costlier required slot rather than an exemption, with a good argument for why exemption clauses spread
Step 1 correctly tries to falsify its own load-bearing assumption before building, and the failure-type table is a useful diagnostic
Strong closing honesty: six anecdotes are not six measurements, and the critic's point that the migration tool may already scaffold a down stub
Concrete five-sessions-plus-control protocol for checking whether the fix stuck
weaknesses: 406 lines with visible sediment: 'Common mistakes' restates five earlier points, 'Order of operations' restates the tiers a third time, and assumption four is flagged four separate times
The pasteable rule is thin (four lines of prose) and the real deliverable is split across five artifacts, so a 30-second skim yields a project rather than something to paste today
Gates the entire fix behind a 20-minute baseline step, adding friction to a question asked as 'how do I make it stick'
Internal tension: 'Six is a pattern. Build the permanent thing' is immediately followed by a step saying do not build yet
Weakest of the two on expectation 4 specifically — placement is framed as tier selection rather than as whether the rule is in context at the moment a migration is written
Spends meaningful space on generic taxonomy about rule forms, which edges toward advice about writing rules rather than the rule
